tests/benchmarks/benchmarks/AuthoringPop.description: Diagnostic (hidden). Incremental spawn SCALING for NVBugs 6664721: one body is authored, sealed, drained and stepped per measured step into an ACCUMULATING attached scene (never reset), so step k is the cost of adding the (k+1)-th body to a scene already holding k. The same single-body author/drain sequence as `Authoring.population_add_drip_cpu` (AuthoringCommon.h), which reloads a fresh scene per step and therefore cannot see growth. endRun() fits cost(k)=a+b*k over 150 spawns (first 3 excluded as warm-up) and prints the ticket's drift metric slope*n/median(Q1) against the 0.50 budget plus quartile medians, so trunk-vs-optimized scaling is directly comparable.

tests/benchmarks/benchmarks/ContactRepor.description: Steady-state contact-sensor net-force read through the session read API (replacing the old raw-contact benchmark rows). Raw event/detail consumers of ovphysx_get_contact_report() migrate through the session contact-event/detail attributes described by ADR-0044; these two aggregated net-force columns do not replace event headers, contact points, or friction anchors. The scene rests 512 dynamic boxes on a static ground; each box carries PhysxContactReportAPI and sleepThreshold 0 so a settled body keeps reporting, making it one contact sensor whose net normal force resists its weight. The step is advanced in preStep() (outside the timer); each sample times ovphysx_query(CONTACT_SENSOR) plus ovphysx_read(netNormalContactForce, netFrictionContactForce) and the drain. The `_gpu` row requires DirectGPU (`--forceGpu --directGpu`) because the net-force columns are device-resident on a DirectGPU scene; under `--forceGpu` alone it is selected and skipped without a metric. Both rows are hidden and run in separate fresh processes.

tests/benchmarks/benchmarks/OutputRead.c.description: Physics-output read vs. tensor-binding read across N bodies/links/DOFs/articulations (cubes20 or cartpole cloned to N envs, or an authored asset for vehicle/particle/deformable families). `queryread_rb` opens, drains, and releases a query every call; `readonly_*` holds the query open across steps, isolating per-frame query cost against `queryread_rb`; `tensorbinding_*` reads the same payload through a persistent tensor binding; `tensorcreate_rb` measures the tensor-binding create+spec+destroy setup the binding amortises. `_gpu` rows require DirectGPU (`--forceGpu --directGpu`) and are hidden. **Residency note:** the output read (`ovphysx_read()` / `ovphysx_fetch_read_next()`) is host-backed even on a DirectGPU scene -- only the tensor-binding destination moves to device memory there (`kDLCUDA`, ADR-0008). The `readonly_*`/`queryread_rb`/`tensorcreate_rb` GPU rows and their `tensorbinding_*` counterparts are therefore NOT like-for-like on residency; read each row's own CPU/GPU delta rather than comparing read vs. binding as a residency ratio.

tests/benchmarks/benchmarks/OutputWrite..description: App-to-physics writes (ADR-0012) at scale through the session write API, against the deprecated tensor binding. `querywrite` rows pay the query, write session, fill, commit and releases every sample, as a stateless caller does; `writeonly` rows hold the query; `writedevice` rows are writeonly rows with the payload already in device memory, so each fill is one device copy and the write waits for its commits, facing the `tensorbinding` rows with the same placement (DirectGPU only); `tensorbinding` rows write the same objects through a binding already built. Some pairs differ in payload width (a position is 3 floats where the binding's pose is 7), so read them as what each API costs to move one attribute; see the README's OutputWrite validity section. The fill is inside the timing: a write session hands the caller its destination buffer. `_cpu` rows run on the default pass; `_gpu` rows need `--forceGpu --directGpu --hidden` in a dedicated process.

tests/benchmarks/benchmarks/WriteScaling.description: `velocity_ovstage_4096_cpu` is the **primary KPI**: a 4,096-body linear-velocity write through OVStage, write completion, query release, velocity-scoped floor, update, and a 1/60s step. `velocity_tensor_4096_cpu` is the comparator: the same step shape but writing a persistent [4096,6] tensor instead. The two use different wait/seal boundaries than the Authoring.* rows above (single-seal-wait vs. separate waits) -- not directly comparable across files; see README's Comparability boundary section. The four hidden `WriteScalingHighN.*` rows are the same fixture at 8,192 and 16,384 bodies with nothing else changed; they carry a separate family prefix so the frozen L1B `WriteScaling.*` selection still returns exactly the two 4,096-body rows, and they are non-paging diagnostics (REQ-CAPI-BENCHMARK-005). The six hidden WriteOnly rows reuse the same CPU fixture and command sequence but stop timing before simulation. They have a separate inventory and require independent threshold calibration (REQ-CAPI-BENCHMARK-007). QueryRetention.velocity_ovstage_4096_cpu retains one query per run across warmup, twenty measured steps and verification; its query setup/retirement are outside timing, while the original WriteScaling/HighN/WriteOnly query lifetimes remain unchanged (REQ-CAPI-BENCHMARK-008).
